intro: Walter Morse Rummel, a pianist closely associated with Debussy, records Chopin’s C♯ minor Waltz in January 1943. The piece moves between a chordal melody, a running refrain and a slower D♭ major song.

sections.label: A · The chordal opening melody
sections.mNote: Long notes alternate with little right-hand flourishes

sections.label: B · Quavers over the waltz bass
sections.mNote: The right hand moves in quick descending phrases

sections.label: C · Song and running replies
sections.mNote: Longer phrases alternate with the descending tune

sections.label: D · The opening melody returns
sections.mNote: Paired notes and short flourishes return in C♯ minor

sections.label: E · The final running tune
sections.mNote: Più mosso leads towards the last C♯ minor chords

cues.title: Two voices in one hand
cues.text: Chopin writes the opening melody in paired notes, with one voice sustained beneath the other. Little flourishes loosen the line; the bass keeps its waltz pattern. The first change of pace, Più mosso, will send the upper voice running down in quavers.
cues.evidence: Score, opening Tempo giusto and first Più mosso; Knute Snortum engraving (2023), p. 1. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An invitation from Paderewski
cues.text: On his way to Paris in 1908, Rummel meets Paderewski in Switzerland. Paderewski likes his compositions and invites him to stay for a year as a pupil. Rummel turns him down and continues to Paris, where he meets Debussy.
cues.evidence: Rummel’s move to Paris, encounter with Paderewski and subsequent association with Debussy: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Morse_Rummel

cues.title: Bach on Rummel’s piano
cues.text: Rummel’s piano also carries music written for other instruments and for voices. He arranges organ works by Bach and Vivaldi, and fills four books with piano versions of movements from Bach’s cantatas. Several singing parts must live under ten fingers.

cues.title: The refrain comes home
cues.text: The quicker tune closes the waltz in C♯ minor. Its slurred quavers keep descending across the bass’s three beats, with upward runs resetting the phrase. The final right-hand leap and left-hand chord bring both hands to rest.
cues.evidence: Score, final Più mosso and cadence, p. 5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
